entries.title: Autonomy is the whole ground you stand on, and unbearable suffering knocks it out from under you. A person in agony isn’t choosing freely — the suffering is doing the choosing; it overwhelms deliberation, narrows the world to the pain, and makes the exit look like the only door. Call that a ‘request’ if you like, but it isn’t autonomous, because no one in that state is the free author of anything. So the autonomy your right rests on is precisely absent in the cases you invoke it for: the more unbearable the suffering, the less free the choice, until at the extreme there is no chooser left to respect — only suffering, asking to end itself.

entries.title: Grant the imposition-debt — that being forced into existence without consent creates a grievance owed compensation. The debtor is still the wrong party. You were imposed upon by your *parents*; they are the agents who acted. *Natalist society owes me a clean death* takes a debt incurred by procreators and bills it to the state, a third party that imposed nothing on you. Take it up with your parents. The state is a bystander you are dunning for someone else's liability — so it owes you nothing, and the claim-right to the means of dying, built on that debt, collapses with it.

entries.title: Legalize assisted dying and the law itself announces which lives society judges not worth sustaining — the disabled, the ill, the dependent. The option's mere availability is a message: that for people so situated, an exit is the intelligible, even fitting, response. Even if no one is pushed, the practice expresses that such lives are worth less, and that expressed judgment is a harm whatever any individual chooses.

entries.text: The objection rides from 'death is irreversible' — trivially true — to 'therefore the irreversibility-asymmetry licenses overriding the choice,' across three premises it never defends. (i) That the… · irreversible · you can't undo it · no taking it back · no second chances · precaution · err on the side of caution · better safe than sorry · what if you're wrong · forecloses every option · can't walk it back · the one choice you can't revise · preserve the option
entries.title: Set aside whether the suffering will lift — grant that it won't, or that no one can know. Death is still the one choice you cannot revise. Every other decision leaves a standing self who can reconsider, adapt, be surprised by a future they couldn't foresee; death forecloses the chooser along with the choice. When one branch is irreversible and the other is not, and you are deciding under uncertainty, the precautionary structure of the situation — not optimism, not the prognosis — favors the branch that keeps every option open. Even a competent, settled agent should defer to that asymmetry, and a regime that lets the irreversible branch be taken has failed to respect it. Better the error you can still walk back.

entries.text: The objection runs together two things a perfect duty-to-self cannot bridge: a first-personal duty the agent might owe their own rational nature, and a warrant for others to obstruct a sovereign exit… · Kant · duty to self · Formula of Humanity · humanity as an end · treat as a means · merely as a means · self-instrumentalization · perfect duty · Groundwork · rational nature · dignity not price · categorical imperative · you can't dispose of yourself · autonomous rational will
entries.title: Kant settles this without a word about sacredness. To end your own life in order to escape suffering is to treat the humanity in your own person merely as a means — you press the bearer of rational agency into service as an instrument for securing relief, and a perfect duty to self forbids exactly that. The wrong is not that you destroy something valuable; it is that the maxim instrumentalizes your own rational nature, the very thing whose dignity grounds all value in the first place. So it holds even if life itself is worth nothing: the prohibition rides on the form of the willing, not the worth of the life, and no degree of misery exempts you from a duty you owe your own personhood.

entries.text: The argument conflates the profession's self-conception with the patient's right: even granting that some physicians regard ending life as outside their role, that fact about medicine's self-image… · medical integrity · first do no harm · primum non nocere · Hippocratic oath · role of the physician · healer not killer · corrupts the profession · erodes trust · conscientious objection
entries.title: Assisted dying violates the integrity of medicine. The physician's role is to heal; 'first, do no harm' is the oath's spine. A doctor who helps a patient die has crossed from healer to killer, corrupts the profession's character, and erodes the trust that makes medicine possible — the patient's confidence that the person at the bedside is unconditionally on the side of their life.

entries.text: The objection vaults from 'this condition can impair some decisions' to 'this person can validly decide nothing about their own life' — an overgeneralization capacity assessment is built to refuse… · can't consent · mentally ill · the illness is talking · not in their right mind · capacity · the depression talking · disorder
entries.title: You can't give valid consent to dying when you're mentally ill — the illness is making the choice, so honoring it isn't respecting autonomy, it's abandoning someone to their disorder.

entries.text: The objection treats palliation as a substitute for permission — assuming the request is exhaustively a demand for pain relief, so any relief a clinician can supply renders it moot — when… · palliative care sufficient · hospice · pain can be managed · terminal sedation · palliative sedation · under-treatment · fix palliative access first · no one needs assisted death · comfort care · refractory symptoms
entries.title: Good palliative and hospice care can control suffering to the very end — terminal sedation reaches even the cases nothing else does. So no one truly *needs* assisted death; they are driven to it by gaps in care. Fund palliation properly and the demand dissolves. Permitting death just lets us avoid fixing what is actually broken.

entries.text: The objection lands the harm principle on its one genuinely direct case — resource subtraction runs through no intervening agency, so directness is conceded, not finessed — then rests everything on… · resource scarcity · medical resource diversion · MAID cost savings · cost of care · hospice beds · palliative capacity · rationing · triage · harm principle · Mill · bystander harm · moral hazard · deadly disincentive · allocation reform
entries.title: Medicine runs on scarcity — a finite stock of palliative beds, clinician hours, hospice capacity, and end-of-life funding, allocated against more need than there is supply. A legal assisted-death program does not draw on some separate reserve; it draws on that same stock. Every assessment, every provision, every clinician trained and hour spent staffing the regime is capacity not spent on a patient who wanted to live and could have been helped. That is harm to others in the plainest form — not a message, not an imitation, but a bed a third party needed and did not get. Mill's principle licenses restricting a liberty that harms others; here the harm is direct, the resource is finite, and someone goes without. Where the diversion is genuinely net-negative for the system and no narrower fix is on offer, the harm-to-others is real and unanswered — and it licenses foreclosing the option.

entries.text: The argument leaps from 'life has (sacred) value' to 'others may forcibly preserve this life against its bearer' — a license that only follows if the sanctity binds the agent without their consent… · sanctity of life · sacred · inviolable · life is a gift · playing God · only God decides · sin
entries.title: Life is sacred and inviolable — ending it is wrong whatever the person wants, and society may step in to honor that inviolability.

entries.text: The slope equivocates on the gating criterion. The right defended is consent-gated sovereign exit; every feared endpoint sorts into one of two boxes. Either it is still a competent person choosing —… · slippery slope · category creep · MAID Track 2 · eligibility expansion · psychiatric euthanasia · Benelux · dementia · Canada MAID · coercion creep · where do you draw the line · the gate widens · non-hypothetical expansion
entries.title: Legalize assisted dying for the terminally suffering and the category will not hold. This is not hypothetical; it is the record. Canada's MAID regime expanded from reasonably-foreseeable death to Track 2 within a few years. Belgium and the Netherlands authorize euthanasia for psychiatric suffering and have moved into dementia. The gate, once cut, widens: chronic illness, disability, the psychiatric, the demented who can no longer consent, the merely tired of life, and at the far end the quietly coerced — the cost-pressured, the burden-fearing, the institutionally nudged. Each expansion is defended in the vocabulary minted for the last. The slope is already greased. The principle you license does not stay where you put it.

entries.text: The objection invokes the harm principle but skips its two preconditions: the contagion death is mediated by the bystander's own agency (failing the directness the principle needs to coerce one… · Werther effect · suicide contagion · copycat suicide · imitation · normalization · baseline suicide rate · harm principle · Mill · behavioral transmission · bystander harm · Papageno effect · responsible reporting
entries.title: Set eligibility wherever you like and freeze it there — the harm is not at the gate. Legalize and normalize assisted death and you raise the baseline rate of ordinary, non-assisted suicide in the general population: the practice models the act, lowers the taboo, and renders self-killing more available to mind. This is the Werther effect, documented for salient suicides, now operating at the scale of the law itself. The dead are not the eligible — they are suggestible bystanders who would not otherwise have died, and they die because the option was made visible and sayable. Mill's own principle licenses coercion to prevent harm to others; here the harm to others is a body count, and the principle bites.

entries.text: The charge conflates a debt owed to others with a license to conscript the agent's continuation — but a debt grounds a claim against the agent, never the right to imprison them. · selfish · selfishness · abandonment · the people left behind · grief · survivors · duty to others · owe it to my family
entries.title: Suicide is selfish — it dumps unbearable pain on the people left behind, who never consented to that grief.

entries.text: The slogan smuggles a universal ('all such problems are temporary') that is empirically false for intractable cases, and even where reversibility is uncertain it conflates the authority to choose… · permanent solution temporary problem · it gets better · it will pass · temporary · reversible · you'll regret it · things change
entries.title: Suicide is a permanent solution to a temporary problem — whatever's driving it will pass, and then the irreversible choice is made on a feeling that would have lifted.

entries.text: The objection reads a choice shaped by social neglect as proof the right launders abandonment, when funding-provision and forbidding-the-exit are orthogonal levers — prohibition removes the option… · cheaper to die · death is cheaper than care · MAID instead of housing · poverty-driven request · can't afford to live · the state offers death not support · manufactured choice · abandonment as autonomy · social neglect · disability and deprivation · Canada MAID poverty · exit instead of provision
entries.title: Make death a legal option and you hand the state an exit from its own obligations. Why fund housing, home care, disability support, mental-health services, when a lethal prescription is cheaper, faster, final? Under real deprivation the “choice” is a fiction: people ask to die because they cannot afford to live — because the supports that would have made life bearable were never funded. The right doesn’t liberate them; it launders their abandonment as autonomy. Look at the Canadian cases: applicants citing poverty, inadequate housing, untreated need. A society that offers its poor death before it offers them care has not expanded freedom. The door must stay shut until that society has discharged its duty to provide.
